docs.title: MemoryLane remembers so you do not have to.
docs.text:
MemoryLane is a personal browser-memory system that captures useful web content and makes it searchable later. Instead of relying on an exact URL, page title, or keyword, you can describe what you remember and search through the content you previously encountered.

Browse
  ↓
Capture
  ↓
Filter
  ↓
Process
  ↓
Store
  ↓
Search
  ↓
Find

docs.title: What MemoryLane can do
docs.text:
• Automatic capture of eligible webpages while you browse
  • Manual capture when you explicitly want to remember a page
  • Content-aware search using natural-language queries
  • Semantic search for meaning-based matching
  • Lexical search for exact terminology
  • YouTube memories using available video transcripts
  • Voice search from the web interface
  • Optional AI summaries for individual results
  • Webpage-level results even though content is stored in smaller chunks

docs.title: Why MemoryLane?
docs.text:
Browser history tells you where you went. MemoryLane is designed to help you remember what was there.

For example, instead of remembering an exact page or phrase, you can search for something like:

"that article explaining how database query latency can be reduced"

MemoryLane searches the content it has stored and returns the webpages whose content best matches the query.

docs.title: Main components
docs.text: Component Role Browser extension Captures and sends webpage content FastAPI backend Coordinates processing and API requests Content processing Cleans, validates, and chunks captured content Sentence Transformer Creates semantic representations Apache Solr Stores memories and performs search Svelte frontend Provides the search interface Gemini Optionally summarizes selected results

docs.title: Browser Extension
docs.text: The Chrome extension automatically captures webpage information during browsing.

docs.title: Content Extraction
docs.text: Webpage content is cleaned and processed to remove unnecessary information.

docs.title: AI Summarization
docs.text: AI models generate summaries of stored webpages.

docs.title: Semantic Search
docs.text:
Users can search memories using natural language queries.

Example:

"Find documentation about ROS navigation"

docs.title: Memory Dashboard
docs.text:
The web application provides:

  • Search interface
  • Browsing timeline
  • Stored memories
  • Categories and tags

docs.title: User Authentication
docs.text: Users can securely manage their personal browsing memories.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: MemoryLane deals with personal browsing information, so privacy is an important part of the system design.

docs.title: Automatic capture filtering
docs.text:
Automatic capture does not blindly submit every browser page to the backend.

The eligibility rules exclude categories such as:

  • Social-media pages
  • Banking and financial services
  • Login and authentication pages
  • Account, checkout, billing, payment, and wallet paths
  • Internal browser pages
  • Search-engine result pages
  • Utility pages
  • Common non-text resources

The filtering is applied by the browser extension before an automatically captured page is posted to the backend.

docs.title: Stored browsing content
docs.text:
A MemoryLane memory can contain the extracted textual content of a webpage, along with metadata such as its URL, title, domain, timestamp, and embeddings.

This means the local MemoryLane data store should be treated as sensitive personal data.

docs.title: Gemini summarization
docs.text:
Gemini is optional and is not required for the core retrieval pipeline.

When Gemini-based summarization is enabled, content used for summarization can be sent to an external API. This introduces a privacy consideration that does not apply in the same way to purely local retrieval.

Sensitive pages or content should therefore not be sent to an external summarization service unless the user is comfortable with the associated data-handling implications.

docs.title: Privacy direction
docs.text: A future privacy-oriented direction for MemoryLane is greater local-first processing and storage, reducing the need to send personal browsing content to external services.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Users frequently consume information online but struggle to retrieve it later.

Students, developers, researchers, and professionals often read useful resources but forget:

  • Website names
  • URLs
  • Exact keywords
  • Where the information was found

docs.title: Browser History
docs.text: Browser history requires users to remember website names or keywords.

docs.title: Bookmarks
docs.text: Bookmarks require manual saving and organization.

docs.title: Search Engines
docs.text: Search engines retrieve information from the internet, not from the user's personal browsing history.

docs.title: Proposed Solution
docs.text:
MemoryLane creates an AI-powered memory layer over browsing activity.

Instead of searching using exact keywords, users can describe what they remember.

Example:

"Find that article about reinforcement learning I read last week"

MemoryLane retrieves the relevant webpage.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: MemoryLane exposes a small FastAPI interface for health checks, memory ingestion, search, and optional summarization.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Endpoint Purpose GET /health Check backend dependencies POST /memory Store a webpage memory POST /search Search stored memories POST /summarize Summarize a selected memory

The API models are defined in backend/models.py.

See API Endpoints for request and response details.

docs.title: GET /health
docs.text:
Checks the availability of the main backend dependencies.

The response reports:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "solr": true,
  "embedding_model": true,
  "gemini": true
}

gemini may be false when optional Gemini functionality is not configured or available.

docs.title: POST /memory
docs.text: Stores a webpage as a MemoryLane memory.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
{
  "url": "https://example.com/article",
  "title": "Example Article",
  "content": "Article content...",
  "canonical_url": "https://example.com/article",
  "is_manual": false
}

docs.title: Processing
docs.text: The backend validates the URL, normalizes it, creates a webpage identifier, handles supported YouTube URLs, chunks the content, generates embeddings, and indexes the resulting chunks in Solr.

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
The response contains:

  • success
  • message
  • metadata

The metadata includes the URL, title, generated ID, chunk count, and timestamp.

docs.title: POST /search
docs.text: Searches stored memories.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
{
  "query": "documentation about ROS navigation",
  "num_results": 5,
  "summarize": false,
  "debug": false
}

num_results accepts values from 1 to 20.

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
A search response contains the original query and a list of webpage-level results.

Each result includes:

  • rank
  • ID
  • title
  • URL
  • domain
  • timestamp
  • optional summary

The debug option can expose retrieval scores for development and analysis.

docs.title: POST /summarize
docs.text: Requests a summary for a selected memory.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
{
  "query": "What are the main ideas?",
  "id": "memory-id"
}

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
{
  "id": "memory-id",
  "summary": "..."
}

The summarization path uses Gemini when the service is available.

docs.title: main.py
docs.text: Defines the FastAPI application and API endpoints. It coordinates memory ingestion, search, health checks, and summarization.

docs.title: models.py
docs.text: Defines Pydantic request and response models used by the API.

docs.text: Handles URL normalization and deterministic webpage ID generation.

docs.title: page_filter.py
docs.text: Contains the URL eligibility rules used for automatic capture.

docs.title: chunking.py
docs.text: Converts long text into chunks suitable for embedding and retrieval.

docs.title: embeddings.py
docs.text: Loads and uses the Sentence Transformer embedding model.

docs.title: summarizer.py
docs.text: Handles optional Gemini-based summarization.

docs.title: config.py
docs.text: Contains application and retrieval configuration values.

docs.title: Frontend Architecture
docs.text: The MemoryLane frontend is built with Svelte, Vite, and JavaScript.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
The frontend provides:

  • Natural-language search
  • Search result display
  • Page title, URL, and domain information
  • Voice search input
  • On-demand result summarization

docs.title: Main structure
docs.text:
Important frontend files include:

frontend/
├── src/
│   ├── App.svelte
│   ├── api.js
│   ├── main.js
│   ├── stores.ts
│   ├── utils.js

├── package.json

The frontend communicates with the FastAPI backend through the configured Vite development proxy.

The frontend is intentionally separate from the backend's processing and retrieval logic.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
MemoryLane consists of four main application areas:

┌─────────────────────┐
│   Browser Extension │
│   Capture + Filter  │
└──────────┬──────────┘
           │ HTTP / JSON
           ▼
┌─────────────────────┐
│    FastAPI Backend  │
│ Processing + Search │
└───────┬───────┬─────┘
        │       │
        ▼       ▼
┌───────────┐ ┌───────────────┐
│  Solr     │ │ Gemini        │
│ Storage + │ │ Optional      │
│ Search    │ │ Summarization │
└───────────┘ └───────────────┘
        ▲
        │
┌───────┴──────────────┐
│    Svelte Frontend   │

└──────────────────────┘

docs.title: Browser extension
docs.text: Responsible for collecting page information, applying automatic-capture eligibility rules, and sending eligible content to the backend.

docs.title: FastAPI backend
docs.text: Acts as the application layer. It exposes the API, processes memories, creates embeddings, communicates with Solr, performs retrieval, and coordinates optional summarization.

docs.title: Svelte frontend
docs.text: Provides the browser-facing search experience, result display, voice input, and summary interactions.

docs.title: Apache Solr
docs.text: Stores chunk-level memories and supports both textual and vector retrieval.

docs.title: Gemini
docs.text: Provides optional result summarization when configured.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text: The architecture separates collection from processing and presentation. The browser does not perform indexing or search itself; the backend coordinates those operations.

docs.title: Processing Architecture
docs.text: MemoryLane's processing pipeline turns captured browser content into searchable memory.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Captured content
      ↓
URL validation
      ↓
URL normalization
      ↓
Webpage ID generation
      ↓
Content validation
      ↓
YouTube transcript handling (when applicable)
      ↓
Chunking
      ↓
Embedding generation
      ↓
Solr indexing

docs.title: URL identity
docs.text: The normalized URL is used to generate a deterministic webpage identifier. This identifier is the link between all chunks belonging to one logical webpage.

docs.title: Normal webpage content
docs.text: For ordinary pages, extracted text is validated and then divided into chunks before embeddings are generated.

docs.title: YouTube content
docs.text: For supported YouTube URLs, the backend retrieves an available transcript and uses the resulting text as the content to be chunked and embedded.

docs.title: Re-indexing
docs.text: If an existing webpage needs to be replaced, the backend can remove the old chunks associated with its webpage identifier before storing the new representation.

docs.title: Retrieval Architecture
docs.text:
MemoryLane supports two complementary forms of retrieval:

  1. Lexical retrieval for words and terminology that directly match stored content.
  2. Semantic retrieval for content that is conceptually related even when different words are used.

docs.title: Lexical retrieval
docs.text:
Solr's eDisMax query mechanism searches the text field and gives the title field additional importance.

BM25 provides the lexical relevance score.

Query
  ↓
Solr eDisMax
  ↓
text + title
  ↓
BM25 candidates

docs.title: Semantic retrieval
docs.text:
The search query is converted into the same 384-dimensional embedding space used for stored chunks.

Solr then performs K-nearest-neighbour retrieval over the dense vectors.

Query
  ↓
all-MiniLM-L6-v2
  ↓
384-dimensional vector
  ↓
Solr KNN

docs.title: Candidate generation
docs.text: The current configuration retrieves up to 30 candidates from each retrieval source.

docs.title: Combining scores
docs.text:
For the production search configuration, the two score lists are normalized independently using min-max normalization.

For a score \(s_i\):

\[ s_i' = \frac{s_i-s_{\min}} {s_{\max}-s_{\min}} \]

The normalized scores are then combined using the configured weights:

\[ S = 0.5S_{\mathrm{BM25}} + 0.5S_{\mathrm{vector}} \]

A document that appears in only one source receives zero for the missing source.

docs.title: Webpage-level ranking
docs.text:
Retrieval happens at chunk level, but users should not see the same webpage repeatedly.

MemoryLane groups candidates using webpage_id. The highest-scoring chunk represents each webpage, and those webpage-level results are returned to the frontend.

Chunk retrieval
      ↓
Webpage grouping
      ↓
Best chunk per webpage
      ↓
Webpage ranking
      ↓
Final results

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: MemoryLane includes automated tests for important backend behaviors.

docs.title: Test areas
docs.text:
The current test suite covers areas including:

  • URL normalization
  • Chunking behavior
  • Retrieval behavior
  • API behavior

Representative test files are:

tests/
├── test_api.py
├── test_chunking.py
├── test_retrieval.py
└── test_url_normalization.py

docs.title: What the tests protect
docs.text:
URL tests verify normalization and deterministic webpage identifiers.

Chunking tests verify that text is divided according to the configured rules.

Retrieval tests cover score normalization, score fusion, and webpage grouping.

API tests cover backend endpoint behavior.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The repository also contains a retrieval evaluation pipeline under evaluation/. It evaluates BM25-only, vector-only, and combined retrieval configurations using retrieval metrics.

The evaluation is separate from the normal automated unit tests.

docs.title: Evaluation Methodology
docs.text: MemoryLane's retrieval implementation was evaluated using the SciFact information-retrieval dataset adapted to the MemoryLane data model.

docs.title: Evaluation corpus
docs.text:
The evaluation setup used:

  • 1,000 unique documents
  • 100 evaluation queries
  • 106 relevant documents in the selected relevance data

The documents were passed through the actual MemoryLane /memory endpoint rather than being inserted directly into Solr.

This means the benchmark exercised the application's processing pipeline, including URL handling, content processing, chunking, embedding generation, and indexing.

docs.title: Benchmark URLs
docs.text:
The benchmark documents use synthetic URLs of the form:

https://scifact.org/doc/{document_id}

These URLs provide unique identifiers for the evaluation documents. The actual document titles and scientific content originate from SciFact.

The experiment is therefore a controlled retrieval benchmark rather than a live-web crawling evaluation.

docs.title: Configurations
docs.text: Three retrieval configurations were compared:

docs.title: BM25 Only
docs.text: Uses lexical retrieval without the semantic contribution.

docs.title: Vector Only
docs.text: Uses dense semantic retrieval without the lexical contribution.

docs.title: Combined Retrieval
docs.text: Uses the production configuration combining lexical and semantic retrieval signals.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The evaluation reports:

  • MRR@10 — how early the first relevant result appears.
  • Recall@10 — how much of the relevant set is retrieved in the top ten.
  • nDCG@10 — the quality of the ranking of relevant results.

Relevance was binary for this experiment.

docs.title: Evaluation Results
docs.text:
The retrieval evaluation produced the following results.

Method MRR@10 Recall@10 nDCG@10 BM25 Only 0.6482 0.8117 0.6776 Vector Only 0.7795 0.8867 0.8008 Combined Retrieval 0.7538 0.9167 0.7890

docs.title: BM25
docs.text: BM25 provides a useful lexical baseline and remains effective when query terminology matches stored content.

docs.title: Vector retrieval
docs.text: Vector retrieval achieved the highest MRR@10 and nDCG@10 on the selected benchmark. This indicates strong performance in placing relevant scientific content near the top of the ranking.

docs.title: Combined retrieval
docs.text:
Combined retrieval achieved the highest Recall@10. It retrieved the largest proportion of relevant documents within the top ten.

The results therefore do not show one method winning every metric. Different retrieval approaches have different strengths on the selected corpus and queries.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
This section follows MemoryLane from browser capture through processing, storage, and search.

  • System Overview
  • Capturing Web Content
  • Content Processing
  • Storage

docs.title: Capturing Web Content
docs.text: The browser extension is the collection layer of MemoryLane.

docs.title: Capture process
docs.text:
When a page is eligible for capture, the extension extracts readable content from the page. It can obtain content through the content script and has an injection-based fallback when required.

The extracted data sent to the backend includes:

  • URL
  • Page title
  • Textual content
  • Canonical URL when available
  • Whether the capture was manual

docs.title: Content extraction
docs.text:
The extension works from a clone of the page body and removes elements that generally do not represent the main readable content, including:

  • script
  • style
  • noscript
  • nav
  • footer
  • aside
  • header
  • common navigation, menu, sidebar, and advertisement elements

The resulting text is sent to the backend for further processing.

docs.title: Duplicate prevention
docs.text:
The extension keeps track of recently captured URLs and captures currently in progress. This prevents repeated submissions for the same URL in a short period.

The backend also checks whether the normalized webpage already exists before indexing it.

docs.title: Backend ingestion
docs.text:
The /memory endpoint then:

  1. Validates the URL.
  2. Normalizes the URL.
  3. Generates a deterministic webpage identifier.
  4. Checks for an existing webpage.
  5. Handles YouTube videos when applicable.
  6. Validates the content.
  7. Chunks the content.
  8. Generates embeddings.
  9. Removes outdated chunks for the same webpage when needed.
  10. Stores the resulting chunks and metadata in Solr.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text: MemoryLane is organized as a pipeline connecting the browser, frontend, backend, content-processing layer, search index, and retrieval system.

docs.title: Memory ingestion
docs.text:
Browser Page / YouTube Video
          ↓
    Browser Extension
          ↓
     Capture / Filter
          ↓
        FastAPI
          ↓
    URL Normalization
          ↓
   Content Processing
          ↓
       Chunking
          ↓
      Embeddings
          ↓
      Apache Solr

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
User Query
          ↓
   Svelte Frontend
          ↓
        FastAPI
          ↓
   Candidate Retrieval
          ↓
        Ranking
          ↓
 Webpage-level Results

docs.title: Separation of responsibilities
docs.text:
The system separates:

  • Collection — browser extension
  • Presentation — Svelte frontend
  • Application logic — FastAPI
  • Representation — Sentence Transformer embeddings
  • Storage and search — Apache Solr
  • Retrieval and ranking — backend retrieval module
  • Optional summarization — Gemini integration

This separation keeps the browser, user interface, processing, storage, and retrieval concerns independent.

docs.title: Content Processing
docs.text: MemoryLane transforms captured content into smaller searchable units before storing it.

docs.title: URL normalization
docs.text:
URLs can have multiple representations that refer to the same logical resource.

MemoryLane normalizes URLs by handling details such as:

  • Scheme and hostname normalization
  • Removing the www prefix
  • Removing default ports
  • Removing fragments
  • Removing common tracking parameters
  • Normalizing trailing slashes
  • Sorting query parameters

A deterministic webpage identifier is generated from the normalized URL.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Very short or invalid content is not treated as a useful webpage memory.

For ordinary webpages, the extension also avoids sending pages with insufficient extracted text during automatic capture.

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
Large pages are divided into smaller chunks.

The configured target range is approximately 300–500 words. Paragraph boundaries are used where possible. Oversized paragraphs can be split at sentence boundaries, with further word-based splitting when a single sentence is still too large.

Very small trailing chunks may be merged back into the preceding chunk.

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
Each chunk is converted into a dense vector using:

all-MiniLM-L6-v2

The model produces a 384-dimensional representation.

The vectors are normalized and used with cosine similarity for dense retrieval.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Chunks retain their relationship to the original webpage through fields such as:

  • webpage_id
  • URL
  • Domain
  • Title
  • Chunk identifier
  • Total chunk count
  • Timestamp
  • Embedding

docs.title: Storing Memories
docs.text:
Apache Solr is the storage and search engine used by MemoryLane.

The project runs an Apache Solr 9.7 instance with a memorylane core.

docs.title: Why Solr?
docs.text: Solr provides the search infrastructure needed by MemoryLane in one system. It supports the textual search, dense-vector search, indexing, and document management required by the application.

docs.title: Document model
docs.text:
MemoryLane stores individual chunks as Solr documents.

Each document contains information including:

Field Purpose id Unique chunk document identifier webpage_id Associates chunks with one webpage url Normalized webpage URL domain Webpage domain title Page title text Chunk text chunk_id Position of the chunk total_chunks Number of chunks for the webpage timestamp Storage timestamp embedding 384-dimensional dense vector

The Solr schema uses a dense vector field for the stored embeddings.

docs.title: Webpage identity
docs.text:
The webpage_id is derived deterministically from the normalized URL. This lets the system manage all chunks belonging to one webpage as a single logical memory.

When a webpage is reprocessed, older chunks associated with that webpage can be removed before the new chunks are stored.

docs.title: Automatic Capture
docs.text:
MemoryLane can capture eligible webpages automatically while the browser is being used.

The Chrome extension supports two capture modes:

  • Automatic — eligible pages are captured when loading completes.
  • Manual — pages are saved explicitly through the extension.

docs.title: Automatic capture flow
docs.text:
When automatic mode is enabled, the extension watches for completed page loads.

Page finishes loading
        ↓
Check capture eligibility
        ↓
Extract readable content
        ↓
Send eligible content to /memory
        ↓
Process and store the memory

The extension also avoids repeatedly submitting the same URL within a short period and prevents duplicate in-flight captures.

docs.title: What automatic capture filters
docs.text:
Automatic capture is deliberately more selective than simply saving every URL.

The eligibility rules exclude categories such as:

  • Social-media sites
  • Banking and financial services
  • Login, authentication, account, checkout, billing, and payment paths
  • Browser and internal browser URLs
  • Search-engine result pages
  • Utility pages such as error, privacy, terms, cookie, and sitemap pages
  • Common non-text resources such as images, media, archives, and executable files

YouTube receives special handling because supported video pages can be stored through their transcripts.

docs.title: Content threshold
docs.text:
For ordinary webpages, automatic capture requires enough extracted text to be useful. Pages with very little readable content are skipped.

Manual capture can bypass the automatic eligibility filtering when the user explicitly chooses to remember a page.

docs.title: Why filtering matters
docs.text: Automatic capture is intended to make MemoryLane useful without turning every browsing action into a stored memory. Filtering reduces unnecessary content and helps keep sensitive or low-value pages out of the memory collection.

docs.title: Searching Memories
docs.text: MemoryLane provides a natural-language search interface for previously stored web content.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Enter a description of the information you remember and submit the query.

For example:

Find the documentation I read about ROS navigation

or:

article explaining ways to reduce database query latency

The query does not have to reproduce the exact wording used by the original page.

docs.title: What happens after a search
docs.text:
Natural-language query
        ↓
FastAPI search endpoint
        ↓
Candidate retrieval
        ↓
Ranking
        ↓
Webpage-level results

The search system can use both exact terminology and semantic similarity to identify useful memories.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Results are presented as webpages rather than individual internal chunks.

A result contains information such as:

  • Rank
  • Page title
  • URL
  • Domain
  • Timestamp
  • Optional summary

The frontend can also request an on-demand summary for an individual result.

docs.title: Search result count
docs.text:
The API accepts a requested result count between 1 and 20. The default is 5.

The internal retrieval process may consider more candidate chunks before producing the final webpage-level list.

docs.title: Summarization
docs.text: MemoryLane provides optional AI-powered summarization for search results.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Summarization is separate from the core retrieval process.

Search
  ↓
Retrieve webpage
  ↓
Request summary
  ↓
Gemini
  ↓
Display summary

The /search endpoint can request summaries, and the frontend can also request a summary for an individual result.

docs.title: Gemini
docs.text:
The summarization component uses the Gemini API when Gemini is configured and available.

The backend also exposes Gemini availability through the /health endpoint.

docs.title: Detail level
docs.text: The summarization system can determine an appropriate level of detail from the query before generating the summary.

docs.title: Privacy consideration
docs.text: Unlike local indexing and retrieval, Gemini-based summarization can send browsing content to an external service. Avoid enabling external summarization for content that should remain entirely local unless the privacy implications are acceptable.

docs.title: Voice Search
docs.text:
The MemoryLane web interface supports voice input for search queries.

A microphone control is available alongside the normal search field.

docs.title: Using voice search
docs.text:
1. Activate the microphone control.
  2. Speak the query.
  3. The recognized text is placed into the search field.
  4. Submit the query normally.

Voice search is an alternative input method; the resulting text is processed through the same search interface as a typed query.

docs.title: YouTube Memories
docs.text: MemoryLane can store supported YouTube videos by using their available transcripts as the textual representation of the video.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
YouTube URL
    ↓
Detect video
    ↓
Retrieve transcript
    ↓
Create textual content
    ↓
Chunk
    ↓
Generate embeddings
    ↓
Store in Solr

For a recognized YouTube video URL, the backend attempts to retrieve the video's transcript instead of treating the video-player page itself as ordinary webpage text.

The transcript is then processed through the same general pipeline used for other memories.

docs.title: Video metadata
docs.text:
The stored textual representation can include information such as:

  • Video title
  • Channel
  • Duration when available
  • YouTube as the source
  • Transcript text

docs.title: Transcript availability
docs.text: Transcript retrieval depends on the video having an accessible transcript. If a transcript cannot be retrieved, the video cannot be converted into a searchable textual memory through this path.

docs.title: Automatic capture
docs.text: Automatic capture applies additional YouTube checks. For example, very long videos may be skipped during automatic capture, while manually requested capture can use the manual path.
